About this project

A concept launch plan for a fictional Austin studio

My goal was to show how a new boutique studio could find an open position in a crowded Austin fitness market and turn it into a practical launch plan. I handled every part of it: competitor research, brand strategy, content planning, and the design and build of this page. I reviewed competitor websites, then hand-built the page in HTML/CSS in VS Code, using Claude Code as an AI assistant. I completed it in September 2026.

At a glance

The short version

I reviewed the websites of Barry's, Pure Barre and CorePower Yoga, including their Austin pages. Here's what I found and what it means for Pulse & Flow.

The opportunity

Nobody in Austin sells intensity and recovery as one class

Barry's is all effort. Pure Barre is all low impact. CorePower offers both, but as separate classes. Pulse & Flow's 30 + 15 format has no direct competitor.

The easy wins

Competitors hide prices and sound generic locally

Two of the three hide their prices. Their Austin pages reuse national copy, and two even name the wrong city. Clear prices and genuinely local content set Pulse & Flow apart at almost no cost.

The watch-out

CorePower is opening on South Lamar

It's selling founding memberships at 25% off for life right now. Pulse & Flow's founding offer should launch soon and be at least as strong.

Recommended first steps
  1. This week: set up the Google Business Profile, launch a founding-member waitlist page, and schedule week 1 of social posts. See quick wins
  2. Weeks 1–4: run the daily Instagram and LinkedIn calendar, moving from awareness to a founding-member launch. See calendar
  3. Ongoing: build partnerships with run clubs, neighboring businesses and local employers instead of paying for ads. See acquisition ideas
01 · Brand positioning

Own the empty corner: high intensity with real recovery

Every big brand in Austin picks one side. Barry's and Orangetheory sell effort. Pure Barre sells low impact. CorePower offers both, but as separate classes you schedule yourself. Pulse & Flow builds the recovery into every class, so one 45-minute booking covers the whole session.

Positioning statement

For Austin professionals who train hard but never make time to recover, Pulse & Flow is the boutique studio where every HIIT class ends in guided yoga recovery. You get the intensity of Barry's and the reset of a yoga studio in one 45-minute booking, so you leave energized instead of wrecked.

How we win against each
Barry's1 studio · W 2nd St

Same sweat, less damage. Barry's has no recovery offer, and its intense branding puts off beginners. Our line: "All the intensity. None of the wreckage."

Pure Barre5 area studios

They're safe and low-impact, but not built for people who want to sweat. Their pricing is hidden behind an account. Our line: "Real intensity, scaled for you. Prices on the homepage."

CorePower5 studios · S. Lamar opening

Our closest rival. Sculpt and yoga come as separate classes you have to book yourself. Our line: "One booking. Both halves. Designed to fit a lunch hour."

PulseEarned intensity

Coach-led HIIT with a scale for every move. Measured, hard and never reckless. Proof: heart-rate zones on screen and scaling options printed on the class card.

FlowRecovery is training

15 guided minutes of mobility, breath and stillness in every class. Recovery is part of the workout, not a bonus. Proof: a named recovery sequence for every class format.

FitBuilt for full calendars

45 minutes, one booking, shower and out. Morning, lunch and evening slots planned around Austin heat and workdays. Proof: public schedule and public prices.

Voice: sounds like
  • Calm confidence: "You'll work. Then you'll breathe."
  • Plain, specific numbers: "45 minutes. 30 hard, 15 restore."
  • Local and warm: parking tips, trail names, heat advice
  • Coach-honest about scaling and rest days
Voice: avoid
  • "Crush it" and "no excuses" hustle language (Barry's territory)
  • Body-transformation promises and before/after photos
  • Wellness jargon without an explanation
  • Promo-first headlines (CorePower's hero is a discount)

Also in the market · Orangetheory

Orangetheory wasn't part of the website review above. It's known for heart-rate-zone interval training (treadmill, rower and floor work), with results tracked in its app and memberships sold through franchise studios across the Austin area. Its gap is the same as Barry's: the session ends at the finisher, with little recovery. I recommend a full review of its Austin pages before quoting its prices or claims.

One Instagram and one LinkedIn post a day for 28 days. Instagram builds the local, visual brand. LinkedIn reaches the same professionals at work, with a founder-led voice and a corporate wellness angle. Start on any Monday. The weeks build from awareness to trust to the founding-member launch.

04 · Landing page

7 website improvements

Each one borrows what a competitor does well or fixes a gap I saw on their sites.

1

A hero that states the hybrid promise, with one CTA

Headline "Strength meets stillness." Subhead "45 minutes: 30 of HIIT, 15 of guided yoga recovery. Every class." One button: Book your first class. Show the intro price on the line under the button.

Evidence: Barry's single repeated CTA works. CorePower's hero is only a discount and says nothing about the brand.

2

Public pricing on the homepage

A 3-column price card (intro offer, class pack, unlimited), plus a founding-member rate and an HSA/FSA eligibility note. No login and no "select a studio."

Evidence: Pure Barre requires an account to see prices. CorePower hides regular rates. Barry's is the only transparent one, and it's expensive ($35 drop-in).

3

Class cards with a Pulse-to-Flow meter

Each format shows intensity (1–5), recovery minutes, and the recovery focus (hips, spine, breath). Use branded names, like "Pulse 30 / Flow 15."

Evidence: CorePower's intensity and heat ratings are the most useful UX I saw. This aims the same idea at Pulse & Flow's positioning.

4

A "Your first class" section with a 30-second video

Cover what to bring, when to arrive, how scaling works, and what recovery feels like. End with "Go all-out or dial it down."

Evidence: Barry's "What to expect" section reduces anxiety. Its brand still intimidates beginners, and we can win them.

5

A live 7-day schedule on the homepage

Embed the booking tool's week view so booking takes 2 taps from landing. With a single studio, you don't need a separate studio page.

Evidence: All three put schedules on per-studio pages, one or two clicks deep.

6

A real Austin location block

Address, parking details, bike and scooter notes, nearest trail, heat-season hours, and a photo of the entrance. Write about the neighborhood in your own words.

Evidence: CorePower South Lamar is the best example (parking, amenities, manager). The other local pages are boilerplate, and two named the wrong city.

7

No popups on first load, and correct local SEO

Show only the cookie bar and move email capture below the fold. Title: "Pulse & Flow | HIIT + Yoga Recovery Studio in Austin, TX." Add LocalBusiness schema and a Google Business Profile with matching name, address and hours.

Evidence: CorePower loads four overlays over its hero, and its Austin page is tagged "Dallas, TX."

05 · Customer acquisition

5 ways to win members that competitors aren't using

None of these showed up on the Barry's, Pure Barre or CorePower websites. All of them run on time and partnerships rather than ad spend.

Cost: free class slots

1. The Recovery Pass for other gyms' members

Anyone who shows a Barry's, Orangetheory, F45 or CrossFit membership gets a free or low-cost Flow-focused class. These people already pay for intensity and skip recovery. Win their recovery days first, then upgrade them to full membership.

How to run it
  • A landing page, "Already train hard? Recover here."
  • Limit it to 1 per person and capture email at booking
  • Follow up on day 3 with a first-month offer
Cost: a coach's time

2. Run-club recovery pop-ups

Austin's run clubs meet weekly, many around Lady Bird Lake. Offer a free 20-minute recovery session right after their run. This puts your brand in front of fit, social, 25–45 professionals.

How to run it
  • Contact 5 clubs and commit to one pop-up a month with each
  • Bring QR cards for a "runners' first class" offer
  • Film every session for week-2 content
Cost: free sampler classes

3. "The 45-minute reset" for Austin teams

Pitch a lunchtime team class to startups and tech offices, with recovery framed as burnout prevention. Offer a group rate, and give each employee a personal referral link that earns them a free class for every friend who joins.

How to run it
  • Use LinkedIn posts (week 2 and 4) as the pitch
  • Message 20 People and HR leads with a free team sampler
  • Track sign-ups by company code
Cost: printed cards

4. The neighborhood recovery passport

Build a 5-stop loop with nearby businesses: coffee, juice, a running store, a massage therapist or PT, and a café. Each gives its customers a Pulse & Flow guest pass. We send our members to them with a perk. A stamp card with all 5 stops earns a free class or a partner reward.

How to run it
  • Walk the block and pitch in person
  • Put a counter card with a QR code at each partner
  • Feature one partner a week on Instagram
Cost: event-day staffing

5. Festival and event recovery classes

Austin's calendar is packed with high-effort weekends: ACL Fest in October, SXSW in March, and big races. Run "Recover from the weekend" classes on the Mondays after. They're timely, shareable, and no competitor owns them.

How to run it
  • Put event dates in the content calendar 3 weeks ahead
  • Offer a special drop-in price with a festival wristband or race bib
  • Pitch the story to local media and newsletters

06 · This week

3 quick wins to ship in the next 7 days

Mon–Tue

Claim and complete your Google Business Profile

  • Category "Fitness studio" plus "Yoga studio," marked as opening soon
  • 10+ photos (build-out, coaches, entrance), hours, booking or waitlist link
  • Name, address and phone that exactly match the website and Instagram

Done when: the profile appears for "HIIT yoga Austin" on Google Maps.

Tue–Thu

Launch a one-page founding-member waitlist

  • The hero line, class anatomy, public prices and a founding-member counter
  • A simple builder (Squarespace, Carrd or your booking tool) plus an email form
  • Correct title and meta ("…Austin, TX") and no popups

Done when: the link is in your Instagram bio and on your Google profile.

Thu–Sun

Start the calendar and book 2 partnerships

  • Batch-create week 1 posts (days 01–07) and schedule them
  • DM 5 Austin run clubs offering a free post-run recovery pop-up
  • Visit 3 neighboring businesses to pitch the recovery passport

Done when: 7 posts are scheduled and 1 pop-up date is confirmed.
